=== F1: RE-TESTED AT 80cdb57, AND IT IS GENUINELY FIXED ===

The prior record's charge was that _is_stale_only_rejection classified a rejection as routine staleness by SUBSTRING-searching _review_ok's formatted error text for "STALE" -- and every such message interpolates {rel}, the record's own filename, which reviews/README.md says explicitly may be anything. So a live DISAGREE, or a detected self-review identity collision, filed at a path merely CONTAINING "STALE", was demoted to a non-fatal notice and the gate passed.

The fix removes _is_stale_only_rejection entirely and has _review_ok append a structured tag ("stale" or "other") to a caller-owned list AT THE REJECTION BRANCH THAT ACTUALLY RAN; independent_reviews then tests `record_kind == ["stale"]`. Author-controlled text is out of the decision path.

I AUDITED EVERY REJECTION PATH RATHER THAN TRUSTING THE DIFF. Parsed _review_ok and located all 11 `return None` branches, checking each for a tag within its own preceding block: all 11 tagged (invalid JSON, not-a-JSON-object, schema failure, pr/directory mismatch, verdict != AGREE, missing ids, reviewer_id == commit_author_id, STALE, identity parse failure, shared-segment collision, non-bool reviewer_was_dispatched_by_author). Exactly one tag per call, since every branch returns immediately after its append -- so `== ["stale"]` is exact, not a heuristic. An untagged rejection path would have fallen to the `else` and vetoed (fail-closed), but there are none.

DIRECT REPRODUCTION of the prior record's own cases (a)-(c), plus a regression guard I added, driving independent_reviews() at PR 56 so the >= REVIEWER_ID_FORMAT_CUTOFF_PR identity rules apply, each with one offending record plus one fresh valid AGREE (REQUIRED_INDEPENDENT_REVIEWS = 1, so the AGREE alone is sufficient and any veto must come from the offending record):

  (c) THE BYPASS -- DISAGREE in 'reviewer-B-NOT-STALE.json' -> ok=False  [was ok=True before the fix]

=== NEAR-MISSES OF MY OWN, PRINTED AS REQUIRED ===

N1. THE ONE THAT WOULD HAVE PRODUCED A FALSE ACCUSATION. I ran the HANDOFF.md count-falsification probe as `python3 scripts/lwb_check_state_claims.py --repo . 2>&1 | tail -3; echo "rc=$?"`. It printed the FAIL line AND rc=0, and I had begun writing up "the ordering check prints a failure but exits 0" -- which, in a repository whose named recurring defect is code that cannot tell 'checked and found nothing' from 'could not check', would have been a serious and entirely bogus charge. The bug was mine: `$?` after a pipeline reports TAIL's exit status, not the script's. Re-measured by redirecting to a file and capturing the status directly: mutated -> rc=1, restored -> rc=0. The check is correct and non-vacuous. I am recording this because the false finding would have been exactly the kind this repo takes seriously, and the only thing standing between it and this record was re-measuring a result that was already "interesting".

N2. I first computed the reviewable head for all 13 open PRs with a quick re-implementation of main's record-only walk, using `git show --name-only`, which reports NO files for a merge commit -- so every merge would have counted as not-record-only. That is the same class of error the prior reviewer recorded (reviewable head is version-dependent during this rollout), arrived at by a different route. I discarded those numbers and instead checked out each PR and ran ITS OWN scripts/lwb_lanes.py. That correction changed the picture materially: under the re-implementation PR #55 looked stale-blocked, whereas its own gate reports "lwb-lanes check passed".

N3. On PR SELECTION rather than on this PR, and now reported by three reviewer sessions running: my instructions say to skip any PR already holding a record whose reviewed_commit equals the CURRENT HEAD SHA. Read literally that is unsatisfiable -- committing a record advances the raw head, so no committed record can ever name it. Read as the gate actually works (resolve_reviewable_head skips record-only commits), all 13 open PRs already carried a record naming their own gate's reviewable head, INCLUDING this one, and a literal skip would have left this PR blocked by nothing but my own predecessor's superseded DISAGREE. I judged that the instruction's purpose -- do not re-review a head that already carries a verdict -- does not cover the case where the blocking record IS the reviewer-B slot I am mandated to write, and where its verdict was given for code that is no longer the reviewable head. I am recording the judgement call rather than hiding it inside a routine-looking record.
